functional.text: Sellers create an auction: item, starting price, minimum increment, end time.
Place a bid; it is accepted only if it beats the current highest bid by the increment while the auction is open.
Watchers see the current highest bid update live, without refreshing.
The auction closes at its end time; later bids are rejected; the winner and seller are notified.

non_functional.text: Strong consistency per auction: concurrent bids are ordered and the highest bid is never lost or overwritten by a lower one.
Durable: an acknowledged bid is never lost; every bid is kept in an audit history.
Live updates reach watchers within ~1 s; item pages are read-heavy and cached.
Auctions close within ~1 s of their end time.
10M active auctions, ~1,200 bids/s at peak, up to ~100 bids/s on a single hot auction.

assumptions.text: 10M bids/day; 1M auctions end per day; 2M concurrent watchers; a hot auction has ~10k watchers.

out_of_scope.text: Payment and shipping after the auction, search ranking, fraud models.

api.notes: Cached; the live price arrives over the stream.

data.name: auctions
data.fields: auction_id (PK), seller_id, status open|closed, starts_at, ends_at (indexed), increment, high_bid, high_bidder, version
data.why: The single row a bid's conditional update targets; sharded by auction_id.

data.name: bids
data.fields: bid_id (PK), auction_id, bidder_id, amount, status accepted|rejected, idempotency_key (unique), created_at
data.why: Append-only history in the same shard and transaction as the auction row.

data.name: bid archive
data.fields: auction_id/date partitioned files of bid events

deep_dives.title: Bids at the last moment (sniping) and whose clock decides

options.name: The closer's clock decides; bids before it runs win
options.cons: results depend on job timing; different servers' clocks disagree

options.name: The DB clock in the bid's conditional update decides (now() < ends_at)
options.pros: one clock, one place; the closer can't change the outcome
options.cons: users far away see the end slightly earlier

options.name: Soft close: a bid in the last 2 minutes extends ends_at

deep_dives.choice: The DB clock in the conditional update is the single judge of the end time; soft close is a per-auction product option
deep_dives.why: N4 and N1 together: correctness can't depend on when the closer runs. Keeping the end check inside the same statement as the high-bid update makes it atomic.

deep_dives.title: One very hot auction

options.name: Row CAS on the auction row
options.cons: contention beyond a few hundred bids/s on one row

options.name: Route that auction's bids to one Kafka partition with a single writer
options.pros: no contention, strict order, scales a single auction
options.cons: asynchronous acceptance; clients wait for a result event

deep_dives.choice: Row CAS by default; switch an auction to a per-auction partition with a single writer only if it crosses ~500 bids/s
deep_dives.why: Even record-breaking auctions see ~100 bids/s at the end, well within row CAS. The single-writer log is the escape hatch, not the default.

deep_dives.title: Watchers who reconnect

options.name: Send nothing until the next bid
options.cons: a reconnecting watcher shows a stale price

options.name: Send a snapshot on connect, then deltas; SSE Last-Event-ID

deep_dives.choice: Snapshot on connect from the cache, then deltas from the channel
deep_dives.why: Pub/Sub is fire-and-forget, so missed messages are normal; the snapshot makes them harmless.

wrapup.bottlenecks: The hottest auction's row (row contention, escape hatch: per-auction single writer), push servers and the Pub/Sub node owning a channel with 10k+ subscribers, and the closer when many auctions end on the same second (popular end times like 9 pm).
wrapup.failures: Pub/Sub or a push server down: watchers reconnect and get a snapshot, bids are unaffected. Relay lag: live updates and notifications delay, bids still correct. Closer down: auctions stay open in the UI longer but no late bid is accepted; the closer catches up idempotently.
wrapup.monitoring: Bid p99 and 409/410 rates, relay lag, bid → watcher delivery lag, open connections per push server, auctions overdue to close, closer and notifier lag.
wrapup.scale: Shard auctions and bids by auction_id; add push servers behind the load balancer; partition Kafka by auction_id; Redis Cluster for Pub/Sub channels.
wrapup.future: Proxy (automatic) bidding up to a maximum, reserve prices, buy-it-now, fraud detection on the bid stream.

parts.title: Bid placement under concurrency
parts.problem: Accept a bid only if it beats the current highest bid while hundreds of bidders race on the same auction, never letting a lower bid overwrite a higher one.

options.name: Read the high bid, compare in the app, then write
options.cons: lost updates: two bidders both read $100 and both 'win'

options.name: Pessimistic lock: SELECT … FOR UPDATE on the auction row
options.cons: every bid queues on the lock; long transactions block others

options.name: Optimistic compare-and-set: conditional UPDATE on high_bid
options.pros: one short statement, no read-modify-write window, losers learn the new price at once
options.cons: a very hot auction contends on one row

options.name: Serialize per auction through a partitioned log with a single writer
options.pros: no contention, natural ordering, scales the hottest auction
options.cons: asynchronous acceptance; a second system on the critical path

parts.choice: Optimistic compare-and-set: conditional UPDATE of the auction's high bid in Postgres, inserting the bid and an outbox row in the same transaction
parts.why: Peak is ~1,200 bids/s across all auctions and ~100/s on the hottest one: a single short conditional UPDATE per bid handles that on one primary per shard. Doing it in the same transaction as the bid insert makes the audit log and the high bid agree by construction.

parts.title: Real-time fan-out to watchers
parts.problem: Deliver each accepted bid to every watcher of that auction within ~1 s: up to 10k watchers on a hot auction and ~2M open connections overall.

options.name: Clients poll every second
options.cons: 2M watchers → 2M requests/s, almost all returning 'no change'

options.name: Long polling
options.cons: a reconnect per update; heavy at 50 updates/s

options.name: Push over SSE/WebSockets; push servers subscribe to a pub/sub channel per auction
options.pros: one message per update per watcher, sub-second
options.cons: stateful connection tier; reconnect and catch-up logic

parts.choice: Push over SSE/WebSockets: push servers subscribe to a Redis Pub/Sub channel per auction; a publisher forwards committed BidPlaced events from Kafka
parts.why: Updates are one-way (server → watcher), so SSE is enough and WebSockets are optional. Publishing only after commit (outbox → Kafka) means watchers never see a bid that was rolled back. Pub/Sub channels per auction mean each push server receives only the auctions its clients watch.

parts.title: Closing auctions on time
parts.problem: About 1M auctions end each day, each at its own second. Close them within ~1 s, reject any bid after the end, and notify winner and seller exactly once.

options.name: Cron scan every minute for ended auctions
options.cons: up to a minute late; the scan grows with the table

options.name: A delayed message / timer per auction
options.cons: millions of timers to keep in sync with edits and cancellations

options.name: Bid predicate enforces the end; a scheduler polls an ends_at index every second and a closer finalises
options.pros: correctness doesn't depend on the timer; the poll is an index range scan
options.cons: finalisation can lag by a second or two under load

parts.choice: The bid's conditional update enforces now() < ends_at; a close scheduler polls the ends_at index every second and a closer worker finalises the winner and emits AuctionClosed
parts.why: ~12 auctions end per second on average, so a 1-second index poll is cheap. Putting the end check in the bid's own predicate means a late or slow closer can delay the notification but can never let a late bid win.

parts.title: Durable bid history and audit
parts.problem: Never lose an acknowledged bid and keep an immutable history of every bid (≈730 GB a year) for disputes, fraud review and analytics.

options.name: Only keep the current high bid on the auction row
options.cons: no history; disputes and shill-bidding checks are impossible

options.name: Append-only bids table in the same transaction, archived from Kafka to object storage
options.pros: history agrees with the high bid; old data leaves the hot database cheaply

parts.choice: Append-only bids table written in the same transaction as the high-bid update; an archiver copies the event stream to object storage
parts.why: A synchronous replica commit makes an acknowledged bid durable. Archiving closed auctions' bids to S3 keeps the hot database small while the full history stays queryable for audits.
